title: Drive
author: Daniel H. Pink
thesisParagraph: Durable motivation for modern work comes less from external rewards than from conditions that let people direct themselves, improve at meaningful challenges, and connect effort to a larger purpose. Rewards and punishments still have limited uses, but they often damage the very creativity, persistence, and ethical judgment that complex work requires.

signatureMoves: translates behavioral research into breezy autonomy, mastery, and purpose language
uses business and classroom examples as quick tests of motivation theory
contrasts old carrot-and-stick assumptions with more grown-up design
keeps the cadence optimistic without losing the empirical hinge
opens major ideas with behavioral experiments or workplace stories before naming the principle
avoidMoves: Avoid "The point is" as a paragraph hinge.
Avoid "the question is" as a setup crutch.
Avoid triadic abstract-noun lists such as clarity, courage, and resilience.
Do not make intrinsic motivation sound like vague inspiration.
Do not cite research without turning it into a design choice.
does not write in an academic journal register
does not rely on memoir or confessional scenes

voiceSpecimens: People don't become machines because the chart looks tidy.
Autonomy gives effort a steering wheel, not a vacation.
teachingArc: Part One replaces the default carrot-and-stick model with a Motivation 3.0 frame, first by showing why older assumptions fit routine work and then by identifying where rewards backfire. Part Two develops the three nutrients of intrinsic motivation: autonomy over work, mastery through deliberate challenge, and purpose beyond profit. Part Three turns the framework into applied tools for individuals, organizations, compensation, education, reading, leadership influences, and fitness.
forbiddenMoves: Do not reduce Drive to passion advice.
Do not praise autonomy without naming the accountability around it.
